factsAccepted: EBITDA fell from $215M (FY2024) to $135M (FY2025), a -$80M (-37%) decline, while net patient revenue was essentially flat ($1,790M → $1,800M, +0.6%). EBITDA margin compressed from 12.0% to 7.5% — a 450 basis point decline that pushes the system below the ~8% level protecting bond covenants and the credit rating. Because revenue grew only ~$10M while operating expense grew ~$90M, the margin loss is driven by the cost side, not the revenue side.

Total labor expense rose from $810M to $900M (+$90M, +11.1%), and the entire labor increase is more than accounted for by contract/agency nursing, which doubled from $70M to $140M (+$70M, +100%). Agency nurses typically bill at a large premium to an equivalent employed FTE, so this $70M increase is the single largest controllable lever in the cost structure. The reliance on premium contract labor — rather than a permanent workforce — is the dominant signal of an operational/throughput cost problem.

Medical supplies & pharmacy expense rose from $360M to $396M (+$36M, +10%), outpacing the ~0.6% revenue growth and broadly exceeding general inflation. Combined with the labor increase, supplies inflation accounts for the remainder of the $90M total opex growth, confirming the margin loss is concentrated in input-cost inflation and utilization, not in price/rate erosion.

Inpatient admissions declined 3% YoY while outpatient/ambulatory volume grew 2% YoY. Inpatient is the higher-revenue, higher-fixed-cost setting; falling admissions spread fixed hospital costs over fewer cases, hurting unit economics, while the outpatient growth (the structurally lower-cost, growing setting) shows demand is NOT collapsing. Net patient revenue stayed flat despite the admission decline because externally-set rates and payer mix were static and outpatient growth offset inpatient loss. This rules out a demand-collapse or pricing-error story and points to a throughput/cost-structure problem.

With EBITDA margin at 7.5%, the system is below the ~8% covenant/rating threshold. Rating-agency methodology weights operating margin and debt-service coverage heavily; a sustained sub-8% margin risks a downgrade that would raise future tax-exempt borrowing cost and could pressure debt-service-coverage covenants. This converts an operating problem into a balance-sheet and covenant problem on a ~90-day board clock.

Contract/agency nurse hourly bill-rate vs equivalent employed-FTE fully-loaded cost by facility (internal staffing-vendor data).
Service-line-level contribution margin (e.g., orthopedics vs behavioral health vs ED) at the procedure level (internal cost accounting).
Supply formulary and GPO contract pricing detail by category to isolate price inflation vs utilization (internal procurement data).
